title: Trades on the Road
text:
There was once a man named Gudbrand. He lived on a small farm tucked up on a hillside road far from town, so people called him Gudbrand up the Lien. He and his wife got along so well that whatever he did, she thought it was done just right—there was never any better way it could have been. They owned the place outright, had some savings sitting untouched in their account, and in the barn they had two cows.

One day his wife said, “I think you should take one of the cows into town and sell it, Gudbrand, so we can have a little cash to use day to day. We’re decent people; we should be able to have a few kroner in our pockets like everyone else. That money we’ve saved, we shouldn’t start dipping into it. And honestly, I don’t know what we need two cows for. It’ll be something gained if I only have to milk and water one instead of two.”

Gudbrand thought that sounded both sensible and fair. He loaded the cow into the trailer and drove into town to sell her. But when he got there, nobody wanted to buy a cow—not at that price, not that day. He asked around, waited, tried again, and still no one bit.

“Well then,” Gudbrand thought, “I can just take my cow back home. I’ve got a stall and everything for her, and it’s the same distance back as it was coming.” So he set off for home again.

A little way out of town he met a man who was trying to get rid of an old horse trailer and tack and was talking about switching to something else. Gudbrand figured it might be better to have something that could pull loads and get him places, so he traded the cow for the horse setup.

He hadn’t gone much farther before he met someone who was moving and needed to sell a little used car cheap, just to be rid of it. Gudbrand thought a car was better than a horse setup in this day and age, so he traded again.

Down the road he ran into a fellow leading a big, well-fed pig in the back of a van, saying he’d raised it himself and didn’t have space for it anymore. Gudbrand thought it was better to have a fat pig than a car that might break down, so he traded the car for the pig.

A bit later he met a woman with a milk goat she was rehoming because she was starting a new job and couldn’t keep up with it. Gudbrand decided milk and cheese sounded steadier than pork all at once, so he swapped the pig for the goat.

After that he met a man with a healthy sheep, the kind that practically looked like it was wearing a winter coat already. Gudbrand thought, “Wool and meat—better than a goat,” and traded the goat for the sheep.

Not long after, he met someone with a noisy goose in a crate, complaining the thing was terrorizing the yard and needed to go. Gudbrand figured a goose was simpler than a sheep, so he traded again.
imagePrompt: On a modern rural roadside just outside town, Gudbrand—a well-meaning hillside farmer—stands beside his beater car and open trailer, shaking hands with a man who is handing over an old horse trailer and tack. The cow is being led away in the background, and Gudbrand’s face shows hopeful practicality as he commits to the first surprising trade under a gray sky.

title: The Bet at the Door
text:
Farther along he met a teenager carrying a rooster in a cardboard box, saying it was his granddad’s but the neighbors had complained. Gudbrand thought, “A rooster’s always handy,” and swapped the goose for the rooster.

By then the day had dragged on. Gudbrand was hungry enough that his stomach ached. He stopped at a little roadside place, and in the end he sold the rooster for a couple hundred kroner and bought himself food, because, as he told himself, it’s always better to keep yourself going than to hang on to a rooster.

He walked the last stretch toward home and stopped in at the nearest neighbor’s place. They asked him how it had gone in town.

“Oh, it’s gone so-so,” Gudbrand said. “I can’t exactly praise my luck, but I can’t blame it either,” and he told them the whole thing, trade for trade, from beginning to end.

“Well,” the neighbor said, “you’ll get a warm welcome when you come home to your wife, I’m sure. God help you—I wouldn’t want to be in your shoes.”

“I don’t think it could have gone much worse,” Gudbrand said. “But whether it’s gone badly or well, my wife is so good-natured she never says a word, no matter what I’ve done.”

“I’ve heard that,” the neighbor said, “but I don’t believe it.”

“Want to bet?” Gudbrand said. “We’ve got money saved up at home that we haven’t touched. Will you put the same amount against it?”

So they made their bet. Gudbrand stayed there until evening, and when it started getting dark they went together to Gudbrand’s place. The neighbor stayed outside by the door to listen, while Gudbrand went in.

“Evening,” Gudbrand said as he stepped into the kitchen.
imagePrompt: At dusk outside Gudbrand’s small hillside farmhouse, The Neighbor—a skeptical onlooker—hovers by the front door, leaning in to listen with a tense, wagering look. Gudbrand, dusty and tired from the road, steps through the doorway into the warm-lit kitchen, his posture hesitant as he prepares to explain the day’s swaps.

title: Goat Instead of Pig
text:
“Evening,” his wife said. “Thank goodness you’re back!”

Then she asked how things had gone in town.

“Oh, so-so,” Gudbrand said. “Not much to brag about. When I got to town nobody would buy the cow, so I traded her for a horse trailer and tack.”

“Well, you should be thanked for that,” his wife said. “We’re good enough people to get ourselves around properly like other folks, and if we can manage something like that, we may as well have it. Kids—go help your father get it put away.”

Gudbrand scratched his neck. “I don’t actually have the horse setup anymore. A little farther on I traded it for a used car.”

“No, really?” his wife said. “That’s exactly what I would have done. Thank you for that! Now we can get to town without begging rides, and if it rains we won’t be soaked through. What would we do with horse gear anyway? People would say we were trying to act like some kind of old-time show. Kids—go see about the car.”

Gudbrand cleared his throat. “I don’t have the car either. I traded it for a fat pig.”

His wife laughed. “Well, of course you did. You should be thanked for that too! Now we can put meat in the freezer and have something decent to serve if anyone comes by. What did we need a car for? Then people would think we were getting fancy. Kids—go take care of the pig.”

Gudbrand said, “I don’t have the pig either. A bit later I traded it for a milk goat.”

“Oh, you do everything so sensibly,” his wife said. “What would we do with all that pork at once, if you really think about it? People would only say we eat through everything we have. Now with a goat we’ll have milk, and I can make cheese, and the goat stays with us. Kids—go help with the goat.”
imagePrompt: In the cozy kitchen, Gudbrand scratches the back of his neck while admitting another trade; across from him, Gudbrand’s Wife—steady, good-natured, and fiercely supportive—laughs warmly and gestures with confident approval. Her expression radiates trust as she embraces the idea of a milk goat, turning his uncertainty into relief in the homely evening light.

title: Hunger Turned Into a Win
text:
Gudbrand said, “I don’t have the goat either. I traded it for a good sheep.”

His wife clapped her hands. “No! That’s exactly how I’d want it—exactly as if I’d been there myself. What would we do with a goat? I’d be chasing it up and down the hillside every evening. With a sheep we can have wool and warm things, and food too. Kids—go see about the sheep.”

Gudbrand said, “I don’t have the sheep now. I traded it for a goose.”

“Thank you for that,” his wife said, as calm as ever. “What would I do with a sheep? I don’t even have the time or patience to be messing with wool, and we can buy what we need like before. But a goose—well, I’ve been craving goose for ages, and the feathers will be nice for a pillow. Kids—go bring in the goose.”

Gudbrand said, “I don’t have the goose either. I traded it for a rooster.”

His wife shook her head, smiling. “Honestly, it’s like you’re reading my mind. A rooster is as good as an alarm clock—up he goes every morning whether you ask him or not. What would we do with a goose? I wouldn’t know the first thing about cooking it properly, and as for a pillow, I can fill one with whatever I have. Kids—go take the rooster.”

Gudbrand said, “I don’t have the rooster either. I got so hungry I had to sell it for a little cash, just so I could eat.”

“Thank goodness you did,” his wife said, without missing a beat. “Everything you do is exactly how I’d want it. What would we do with a rooster anyway? We’re our own bosses; we can get up when we like. As long as I’ve got you home again, who needs roosters or geese or pigs or extra cows?”

Then Gudbrand went and opened the door.

“Have I won the bet now?” he called out, and the neighbor had to admit he had.
imagePrompt: By the open front door, Gudbrand finally blurts out that he sold the rooster for food, his hands spread in apology. Gudbrand’s Wife stands close, calm and smiling, touching his arm in reassurance as if it’s the most sensible choice in the world; outside in the dim yard, The Neighbor is caught mid-reaction, stunned that she still isn’t angry.
